newsitem.title: USA: FTC again rejects Staples merger with Office Depot.
newsitem.headline: FTC again rejects Staples merger with Office Depot.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission on Friday rejected a restructured $4 billion merger of Office Depot and Staples Inc., arguing it would raise prices on office products across the country.
The 4-1 decision sets the stage for the FTC to go into Federal District Court next week to block the merger.
FTC litigator George Cary will argue that if the companies merge consumers will pay millions of dollars more in higher prices.
Staples Chief Executive Officer Thomas Stemberg said it was "highly likely" his company and Office Depot will decide to carry the fight into court.
"We feel very confident there is strong merit in our position," he said at company headquarters near Boston. "I think it's a reasonable conclusion this is going to end up in court."
Office Depot stock lost more than a quarter of its value, dropping $5.625 on the the New York Stock Exchange to $13.375, while Staples gained 62.5 cents to $21.875 on Nasdaq.
Comments by the top lawyer for the FTC made it clear further negotiations would be futile.

"Standing here today in good faith, I don't see a settlement that will solve the problem posed by this merger," William Baer, chief of the FTC bureau of competition, said at a news conference. He called the proposal to merge fundamentally flawed.
The FTC decision marked the second time Staples has been turned down in its effort to merge.
Last month the commission voted 4-1 to reject a proposed merger. Staples and Office Depot then negotiated a plan to divest 63 stores to the third player in the field, OfficeMax Inc.

But when commissioners looked at the data they did not like what they saw. To demonstrate the problems, FTC lawyer Baer displayed two seemingly identical Office Depot colour display advertisements, carried earlier this year in Florida newspapers.
The only difference was the prices.

An Orlando Sentinel ad showed a box of copy paper for $17.99. An ad from the Leesburg Daily Commercial 40 miles away advertised the same paper for $24.99. In all, there were dramatic price differences in five of the six items featured.
Baer said the lower prices resulted from competition from two office superstores in Orlando, compared to no competition in Lessburg.
"If this deal goes through, in more than 40 markets, office supply prices will be a lot closer to those in Leesburg than to those in Orlando," he said. "That is what is wrong with this deal."
In the vote Friday, Commissioner Roscoe Starek dissented. Commissioner Mary Azcuenaga voted with the majority, but only because she held that the companies had a right to merge without conditions.
The key vote was that of Chairman Robert Pitofsky, who was supported by Commissioners Christine Varney and Janet Steiger.
The argument that prices would increase under the deal had been made all along by the Ralph Nader Consumer Project on Technology.

"What the commission did was great," said James Love, an economist with the project. "This was an important case. The fundamental question is: is two (office superstores) enough. Today the commission said no, two is not enough."
It was Love who suggested that the commission open its Web site to comments from the public. The FTC did, and Baer said it recieved about 2,000 comments in 10 days.
The decision leaves three players in the field. Staples and Office Depot each have around 500 stores, while OficeMax has between 700 and 800 stores.
The chief executives of both Staples and Office Depot expressed bitter disapppointment.
Staples CEO Stemberg said, "We do not understand their rationale." Office Depot CEO David Fuente called the decision "absurd."

Staples and Office Depot argued that their competitors extended far beyond the three chains of superstores and included everyone from the corner pharmacy selling school supplies to giant discounters selling computers, furniture and office supplies in bulk.
In addition, the firms argued that their merger would actually lower costs to consumers because of increased efficiencies.
On the NYSE, Office Max stock fell $1.125 to $11.875.
